nodes.title: The tools
nodes.text: How SpecSheriff's own toolset carries out the base of the guidelines.

children.title: Where the files are
children.text: Each domain of the specification is kept under `specs/<domain>/`, opening with its head in `specs/<domain>/00-<domain>.json`, contracts under `specs/contracts/`, the technical appendix under `specs/tech/`, each of its sections in a file of its own — a domain's in `<domain>.json`, the stack's in `stack.json`, the technical debt's in `debt.json` — and the guidelines under `specs/_guidelines/`: the base in `spec.json`, the appendix of the tools in `tools.json`, and a project's own guidelines in `project.json`. A part divided into one file per section keeps its files in its directory. The schema is kept in `specs/_schema/`: `node.schema.json` for a node and its metadata, `section-file.schema.json` for the file of a part. Confirmations are kept in `specs/_confirmations.jsonl`, the archive of removed nodes in `specs/_archive/<name>.json`. `specs/_viewer/` (the map) and `md-version/` (the readable export) are rebuilt after every change to the specification and not stored in git. The toolset is installed as the npm package `specsheriff`, which provides the command `sheriff`, and its plugin for pytest as the package `pytest-specsheriff`. The toolset's settings are kept in `sheriff.config.json` at the root of the repository. Among them, glob patterns name where the system's code lives and where its tests live: the code is read for tags, the tests for the sids they declare, and a file neither names for neither — which is how the repository's tools, its configuration and its tests are exempt from tags by where they live. The repository the core is written in says so by the setting `"writesCore": true`. The documents are the markdown files the repository keeps outside `specs/`. The tools of the specification are the toolset's own files: a project installs them and keeps none of them, and the repository the core is written in keeps them under `packages/`, where the tests are read for the sids they declare and no file is read for an address. The specification's owner is the one the top node of `project.json` names, and the levels its domains stand at are the members of the list carried by the rule of `project.json` that refines §s-nkyty4dy9x2v2a4.

children.title: The commands
children.text: `sheriff validate` runs the checks of the specification on its own, and `sheriff binding` those between the specification and the code, the drift report with them; `sheriff citations` checks the citations outside the specification; `sheriff message` grades a commit message against the file git hands a commit-msg hook, and `sheriff review` asks the reviewer for its verdict on the commit being made. `sheriff reindex` gives a sid to every node that has none, computes every node's address from where it stands, empties every incoming list and rebuilds it from the outgoing ones, rebuilds the index in every domain's head from the domain's sections, and empties the status of every checked node outside the core the project takes unless the latest line for its wording's fingerprint is a confirmation by the node's owner; it is run after every change to the specification. Before anything else, `sheriff reindex` merges, in every file it rewrites, the values an object holds under one key, each into those written before it: two lists into one holding the members of the first and then those of the second that the first does not hold, two objects key by key in the same way with each key where it was first written, and two values JSON Schema holds equal into one. It names every key it merged, with the file and each value's line, and refuses any other two, naming the file, the key and each one's line and value, and then writes no file. `sheriff confirm` records an owner's confirmation (§s-v4qus7raqnwzneb). `sheriff guard` judges an edit an agent is about to make. `sheriff export` writes the readable export in markdown, one file for each file of the specification, and `sheriff render` the map. `sheriff guide` prints every node of the guidelines — the base, the appendix of the tools and the project's own — with its sid, text and reason, and the figures counted off the model as it prints: how many nodes each part holds and how many of them are checked. `sheriff show` prints a node, found by its sid or its address: its address, title, status, text and reason, and every link it makes or receives, named by the address and title of the node at the other end. `sheriff types` generates, from the record nodes, the types and the runtime checks of the system's code, where the technical appendix says they stand.
children.rationale: The reindex rewrites whole the files written by hand, so it keeps everything they hold: two values written under one key are each somebody's intent, kept together where both can stand and refused where keeping one would drop the other, since nothing says which was meant; and every merge is named, because one of them may have been written to replace the other.

decisions.problem: The types and runtime checks generated from the record nodes had no command.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a command of their own generates them.

decisions.problem: The reindex read every file through a parser that keeps the last of two values under one key and drops the first, and wrote back what it read: a ruling written under a second decisions key of a node's metadata hid two earlier rulings on the same rule from every tool, and the next reindex would have deleted them.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the reindex merges the two values, names each merge, and refuses two it cannot merge, naming both.

decisions.problem: A command reported a citation as a candidate for a link nobody typed, and the citation check, which a commit runs, was named by no rule.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's rulings on citations (§s-bpdqd9v72wg7vsz, §s-hr7j7scmfkkjnws): the command reporting candidates goes, and the citation check is named among the commands.

decisions.problem: The commands were one repository's package scripts.
decisions.ruling: The owner: they are the commands of SpecSheriff's toolset, described in the appendix of the tools.

children.title: Building the map
children.text: `sheriff render` reads the nodes and writes into `specs/_viewer/` a web page that draws the map from them. The web page draws it with markmap, from an outline in markdown that the command builds and keeps nowhere. Nothing is written by hand at any step: the map is regenerated from the nodes exactly as the readable export is.
children.rationale: The nodes are already a structure any drawing tool can read, so the map keeps no format of its own between them and the web page: a kept format would be a second copy of the structure, and one that keeps only titles and nesting, dropping the sids, status and links that anything shown on top of the map would be bound to.

decisions.problem: The rule called the file the command writes a page, a word a project may keep for a page of its own user interface.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it is a web page, and the rule says so.

children.title: The hooks
children.text: Each check lives in a command a git hook calls: `.githooks/pre-commit` runs `sheriff export` and `sheriff render`, then `sheriff validate`, `sheriff binding` and `sheriff citations`, `.githooks/commit-msg` runs `sheriff message` and then `sheriff review` on the file git hands it, and `.githooks/pre-push` runs the tests of the system's code. A clone turns them on once, with `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`. At a commit, the checks read what is staged. The agent's hooks described are Claude Code's, kept in `.claude/settings.json` in the repository: before an edit made with the file tools, `sheriff guard` judges it; after any edit, `sheriff reindex`, `sheriff export`, `sheriff render`, `sheriff validate`, `sheriff binding` and `sheriff citations` run over the working tree, its difference from the last commit read as the commit, and what they refuse is reported to the agent. An edit made through the shell is not judged before it is made; the checks after it and at the commit still read it.
children.rationale: A hook runs each check where the commit is made, so that none depends on whoever commits remembering it; kept in the repository and turned on by one setting, the hooks are the same in every clone. The agent's hooks are kept in the repository for the same reason, so that every clone's agent is held by them.

decisions.problem: The citation check was run by no hook, so citations it refused reached the main branch through commits every hook had passed, and nothing checked that a citation in a node had a link.
decisions.ruling: Following the owner's rulings on citations (§s-bpdqd9v72wg7vsz, §s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm, §s-hr7j7scmfkkjnws): the pre-commit hook runs the citation check, and the check of the specification refuses a citation with no link.

children.title: How each check is made
children.text:
How each check is made, and by which command:

| Check | How | Command |
|---|---|---|
| One key twice | the file is read as text, and the keys of each object are counted | `sheriff validate` |
| The schema | the file is validated against the schema with a JSON Schema validator | `sheriff validate` |
| Sids, ids, terms | every sid, id, term and record node's name is collected and counted | `sheriff validate` |
| Addresses | the addresses are computed in memory and compared with what is committed | `sheriff validate` |
| Confirmations | the latest line for the fingerprint of the wording of each checked node outside the core the project takes is looked up in the confirmations, and the owner it names is compared with the node's owner | `sheriff validate` |
| The archive | each sid the commit removes from the specification is looked up in the confirmations, and one a confirmation was ever given for is looked up in the archive, with the reason for its removal; one never confirmed is refused where it stands in the archive | `sheriff validate` |
| Links and citations in the nodes | every outgoing link's target is resolved against the sids that exist, and the citations in every node are read and set against the links it makes | `sheriff validate` |
| Incoming links, heads' indexes | they are rebuilt in memory and compared with what is committed | `sheriff validate` |
| Capitals | the title, text and reason of every checked node are read for two words or more running in capitals, a quoted name left out | `sheriff validate` |
| Order of the domains | the order is computed from the consumes links | `sheriff validate` |
| Levels | the level each head names is looked up in the list the project's own guidelines hold | `sheriff validate` |
| Record variants | the record nodes, their refines links and the choosing fields' lists of values are read | `sheriff validate` |
| The core | the base and the appendix of the tools are compared, file for file, with the core the installed `sheriff` carries, the version of `sheriff` a project installs being the version of the core it names; the repository the core is written in says so in `sheriff.config.json`, and compares it with nothing | `sheriff validate` |
| Appendices and a project's own guidelines | the outgoing implements and refines links of each node are resolved, and the part of the node each names is read | `sheriff validate` |
| Tags | every symbol of the system's code is read for its tag, an inner symbol covered by the one it stands in, and a category exempt by where it lives is not read at all; the commit's changed lines are mapped onto the symbols they fall in, a line holding a tag, before the commit or after it, onto the symbol the tag stands on, and a symbol whose every changed line holds no tag and differs from the line it replaces only in a comment, in the sid a citation names or in an identifier the commit renames throughout counts as unchanged | `sheriff binding` |
| Tests | every test is read for the sid it carries, resolved against the nodes, and the tests whose text the commit changes against the checked ones; the sids of the tags on the changed symbols are looked up among the sids every test carries | `sheriff binding` |
| Lists of code and tests, symbols, lists | the tags and the sids the tests carry are collected across the repository and compared with the metadata, and the members of a list with the declaration it names | `sheriff binding` |
| Addresses outside the specification | the files outside `specs/` and the tools are read for a part's name followed by a place, in any case and whether or not it names a node now | `sheriff binding` |
| Generated copies | the types and the runtime checks are generated in memory and compared with what is committed | `sheriff binding` |
| Drift | the history of the node is compared with the history of the files in its metadata, a renamed file read under both its names | `sheriff binding` |
| Citations outside the specification | each sid in the code, the tests and the documents is resolved, the archive's included, and a number naming a node refused | `sheriff citations` |
| Before an edit | the edit is applied to the file in memory and its changed lines are mapped onto the symbols as the Tags row maps them; the tags of each changed symbol are looked up among the sids the tests of the working tree carry, the edited file as it would stand included, and a node the edit leaves checked is looked up in the confirmations as the Confirmations row does | `sheriff guard` |
| The message | the sids in the message are resolved and set against the tags on the changed symbols | `sheriff message` |
| The review | a runner reads the commit's change against the nodes it names | `sheriff review` |
| The tests | they are run | the project's test command, from the pre-push hook |

decisions.problem: Nothing refused a file whose object holds one key twice. JSON Schema leaves the behaviour of such a document undefined, so it escapes the check that it matches its schema (§s-eferktypcj7njt5), and a tool reading it keeps the last of the two values alone.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the check of the specification refuses it, so a commit cannot carry it.

todos.text: The Record variants row checks a value against the choosing field's own list only: how a project's own guidelines name another place where such values are declared, and so how a variant is found to stand in the domain declaring its value, is to be described, and checked once it is.

children.title: The tag that binds a symbol to its rule
children.text: A tag is the line `@spec <sid>` in the comment directly above the symbol it binds, above its decorators where it has any — in TypeScript and JavaScript its doc comment, in Python a comment line — and a symbol implementing several rules carries several. A symbol that implements no rule says so with `@spec none`, followed by the reason it carries none, and one standing first in a run of re-exports, with no blank line between them, says it for the whole run. The delimiters of the comment may share a tag's line and nothing else may, so that a tag's text is found by a scan in any language. Which symbol a tag stands on is found by parsing the file with tree-sitter and the grammar of the file's language — the parser alone, with no program and no type checker — and a description of each language names what counts as a declaration and as a test in it; TypeScript, JavaScript and Python are described.
children.rationale: A comment above a symbol is where an editor shows a tag and where a reader of the symbol is already looking. A scan finds a tag but cannot see what it is attached to, so a tag standing over nothing would pass it; the parser sees the symbol under the comment, and used alone it answers the same for the same file every time and is cheap enough to run at every commit. One parser with a grammar per language makes a further language a description rather than new code.

decisions.problem: The tag's rule says a tag stands in the doc comment above the symbol it binds, and nothing checked it: the check read tags by scanning, which finds a tag and can say nothing about what it is attached to. A tag naming a rule and standing over a blank line, or trailing a statement, passed. For the same reason the symbols a node names in its metadata were not graded at all, only the files.
decisions.ruling: Where a tag stands is decided by parsing the file — the parser only, no program and no type checker. A tag binds to the declaration below it where no blank line separates them, and a node that names symbols is held to the ones its tags stand on. A language server was refused for the same job: its answer depends on the state of a running server, and the checks require the same commit to get the same answer every time (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh).

decisions.problem: The exemption stood at the top of a file, while s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4 now has every declaration carry its own tag.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the exemption stands on the declaration, and on the first of a run of re-exports for the whole run.

decisions.problem: Which declaration a tag stands on was found by one language's parser alone, so the binding could not be held in any other language.
decisions.ruling: The owner: one general parser, with a grammar per language, reads the code; a language is added by describing what counts as a declaration and as a test in it, and TypeScript, JavaScript and Python are described at launch.

children.title: How a test declares the rule it verifies
children.text: In TypeScript and JavaScript a test declares the sid of what it verifies by opening its name with it: `test("s-… what it verifies", …)`. In Python it declares it by a mark on the test, `@pytest.mark.spec("s-…")`; SpecSheriff's plugin for pytest registers the mark and opens the name a run reports with the sid. The description of a further language says how a test declares its sid there.
children.rationale: A test's name is a string in TypeScript and JavaScript, which a sid can open; a Python test is named by its function, which cannot hold a hyphen, so the sid goes into a mark, and the plugin puts it where a run's report shows it.

decisions.problem: A test bound to its rule by the opening of its name cannot be written in Python, whose names cannot hold a hyphen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: in Python a test declares its sid by a mark on it; each language's description says how a test declares its sid there.

children.title: Who runs the reviewer
children.text: `sheriff review` hands the reviewer's input to the runner named in `sheriff.config.json`, and the runner hands back its answer as JSON: a verdict, pass or refuse, and the findings, each naming the rule, the file, the line and the problem. A runner is started with no tools, none of the user's settings, memory or hooks, a system prompt of its own and an empty working directory, so that nothing of the session that wrote the code reaches it. The runner described is the Claude Code CLI in print mode, asking for the model `fable` and falling back to `opus` where the first is overloaded or not offered; the model, and the time after which a run is ended, twenty minutes unless set otherwise, are settings in the same file.
children.rationale: Print mode answers once and exits, with no session around it to carry anything over. The most capable model is asked for because whether code does only what its rules say is the one judgement among the checks. The limit on a run's time ends a run that hangs rather than hurrying one that reads a large change, which is why it is long.

decisions.problem: The reviewer was one agent's command line.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a runner carries the review out, the Claude Code CLI first, then the Codex and Gemini CLIs, then any service speaking the OpenAI-compatible API, which covers models run locally.

todos.text: Describe the Codex and Gemini CLIs as runners, then any service speaking the OpenAI-compatible API, which covers models run locally.

children.title: How a confirmation is recorded
children.text: `sheriff confirm <sid>...` appends to `specs/_confirmations.jsonl` one line per node — its sid, the fingerprint of its wording and the owner confirming it, who is the email git is configured with — and sets the node's status to checked. It refuses a node whose owner is someone else, naming that owner, and appends nothing for a node where the latest line for that fingerprint is already a confirmation by its owner. `sheriff confirm --withdraw <sid>...` appends a line withdrawing the confirmation of the wording the node holds, and empties its status. Of the lines for one fingerprint, the latest decides. The fingerprint is a SHA-256 hash of one canonical string holding the node's title, text and reason and the values its kind carries beside them, but neither the owner a node names nor what the reindex builds, the keys of an object sorted and a list in its own order. An owner is named by an email.
children.rationale: One line appended per confirmation merges between branches without a conflict and keeps every confirmation ever given, and with the latest line deciding, a withdrawal cannot be undone by typing a status back. SHA-256 is a hash every language provides. The email git is configured with is the one a commit names its author by, so a confirmation and the commit carrying it name the same person. The owner a node names says who reads its wording, not what the wording is, and what the reindex builds is no one's wording.

decisions.problem: Confirmations were kept in one person's files outside the repository, guarded by that person's hooks, so nobody else could check a status and a lost file would have emptied every status.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a confirmation is kept with the specification, names who gave it and is accepted only under that owner's signature.
